manual_review_flags: edō (eat) is not DCC ēdō (bring forth)
magnus standard editorial spelling; DCC source has māgnus
fīlius is a secondary headword in combined fīlia/fīlius row

chapters.title: In hortō
chapters.story: Līvia explores the garden; a small child stands beside a large tree.
chapters.editor_note: Keep an image-led start, with repeated singular descriptions.

chapters.title: Familia
chapters.story: Mārcus, Flāvia, Līvia and Tītus stand before the villa; their relationships are named.
chapters.editor_note: The son fīlius shares one DCC entry with fīlia.

chapters.title: Cēna
chapters.story: At supper Tītus eats bread and Līvia drinks water while Flāvia points to each object.
chapters.editor_note: Accusative comes BEFORE the dative; edō 'eat' and bibō are extra-DCC words, not the core-list ēdō.

chapters.title: Dōnum
chapters.story: Līvia gives her mother a red rose; her father receives another gift.
chapters.editor_note: Visual action clearly shows giver, gift and receiver.

chapters.title: Recēnsiō I — In vīllā
chapters.story: The family retells a short garden-and-supper story with two gifts.
chapters.editor_note: Retell using only vocabulary from chapters I–IV, plus zero new lemmas.

chapters.title: Forum
chapters.story: At the market Mārcus chooses two apples while Līvia counts three on the stall.
chapters.editor_note: Two bought apples versus three displayed must be visually unambiguous.

chapters.title: Canis in viā
chapters.story: A dog runs along a Roman street to Līvia at the gate; a boy calls him.
chapters.editor_note: Keep the current dog story but use non-leading comprehension questions.

chapters.title: Tempestās
chapters.story: The family hears rain and wind; people look out of different windows.
chapters.editor_note: No past tense, future tense, or negative commands here.

chapters.title: Recēnsiō II — Canis redit
chapters.story: A small review tale uses the market, the storm and the running dog.
chapters.editor_note: Reuse the first eight chapters; no unseen verbal endings.

chapters.title: Ego in hortō
chapters.story: Līvia narrates what she sees and carries in the garden.
chapters.editor_note: Build from known third-person clauses.

chapters.title: Tū quid facis?
chapters.story: Līvia asks Tītus what he is doing; he answers directly.
chapters.editor_note: Alternate ego / tū dialogue to prevent memorised forms.

chapters.title: In vīllā et ex vīllā
chapters.story: The children go into the villa and come out from it.
chapters.editor_note: Contrast stative in vīllā with motion ad vīllam already seen.

chapters.title: Recēnsiō III — Ubi sumus?
chapters.story: A dialogue revisits I/you forms and near versus inside locations.
chapters.editor_note: Include a map of the villa rooms with labelled places.

chapters.title: Rosa rubra
chapters.story: The family chooses among red, white, large and small objects.
chapters.editor_note: Use canonical magnus display; DCC māgnus is separately flagged as doubtful.

chapters.title: Amīcī et amīcae
chapters.story: Several visitors arrive at the villa, with different people and gifts.
chapters.editor_note: Keep adjective agreement in plural as recycled extension, not a new system.

chapters.title: Nōs et vōs
chapters.story: Family members plan together; hosts speak to visiting friends.
chapters.editor_note: Say what 'we do' and what 'you all do' in simple repeated sentences.

chapters.title: Recēnsiō IV — Hospitēs
chapters.story: Visitors arrive, eat together, and talk about pictures.
chapters.editor_note: Short independent reading with known persons and plural forms.

chapters.title: Veni hūc!
chapters.story: Mārcus asks Tītus to carry a basket and Līvia to open the door.
chapters.editor_note: Do not include nōlī yet.

chapters.title: Quid vult Līvia?
chapters.story: A child wants to read and can carry a book but cannot reach a shelf.
chapters.editor_note: Introduce one simple finite verb plus infinitive pattern.

chapters.title: Mē vides?
chapters.story: A family member points to themselves and then to another person.
chapters.editor_note: Contrast subject and object pronouns pictorially.

chapters.title: Recēnsiō V — Verba familiae
chapters.story: A short conversation recycles pronouns, plural verbs and commands.
chapters.editor_note: Do not introduce new imperatives, voices or tenses.

chapters.title: Herī et hodiē
chapters.story: Two pictures contrast today's good weather with yesterday's storm.
chapters.editor_note: Build understanding of a past state before narrative past verbs.

chapters.title: Ad fenestram
chapters.story: Tītus was reading while Flāvia was writing during heavy rain.
chapters.editor_note: Keep the past continuous; do not introduce perfect yet.

chapters.title: Nōlī timēre
chapters.story: Flāvia comforts Tītus and tells him not to fear thunder.
chapters.editor_note: Clear calm context and repeated single command pattern.

chapters.title: Recēnsiō VI — Post tempestātem
chapters.story: The family retells how it felt and what people were doing in the storm.
chapters.editor_note: Compare present, imperfect and commands in familiar scenes.

chapters.title: Dōnum parāvī
chapters.story: Līvia reports that she prepared roses and called her mother.
chapters.editor_note: Introduce completed events with a simple timeline.

chapters.title: Nūntius vēnit
chapters.story: A messenger reports what he said, saw and did on a journey.
chapters.editor_note: Only a handful of very frequent non-v perfects.

chapters.title: Liber anteā missus
chapters.story: The children discover that a letter had been sent before the visitor arrived.
chapters.editor_note: Use two clearly ordered past events, not an unintroduced participial construction.

chapters.title: Recēnsiō VII — Litterae
chapters.story: A short mystery reorders past actions and discovers a lost message.
chapters.editor_note: Sentence ordering by time and two short rereads.

chapters.title: Crās in viā
chapters.story: The family will visit friends and carry a gift tomorrow.
chapters.editor_note: Separate this from other future formations.

chapters.title: Iter crāstinum
chapters.story: The children ask what they will see and do on the journey.
chapters.editor_note: Future ībimus can appear as one annotated lexical exception, not a second paradigm.

chapters.title: Cum redierit
chapters.story: The visit will end after someone has returned with the book.
chapters.editor_note: Contrast future events and prior completion in a visual timeline.

chapters.title: Recēnsiō VIII — Iter
chapters.story: The family sets out, travels, and recounts the return.
chapters.editor_note: New narrative built entirely from previously introduced grammar.

chapters.title: In urbe
chapters.story: The family meets a person near the river in a large city.
chapters.editor_note: Contrast homō/hominem, canis/canem and city terms in short clauses.

chapters.title: Quī librum habet?
chapters.story: A visitor who lives nearby brings back a missing book.
chapters.editor_note: Start with subjects in simple relative clauses.

chapters.title: Hic an ille?
chapters.story: Līvia distinguishes two baskets and the people who own them.
chapters.editor_note: Build a controlled this/that contrast using two pictures.

chapters.title: Recēnsiō IX — Cuius liber?
chapters.story: The family identifies lost property by its owner and location.
chapters.editor_note: No passive participles or extra case paradigms in this review.

chapters.title: Vocātur
chapters.story: At the forum people are summoned, and goods are sold.
chapters.editor_note: Pair active and passive depictions side by side.

chapters.title: Dōnum repertum est
chapters.story: The family learns that a lost object has been found.
chapters.grammar_focus: Perfect passive participle + sum as a verb
chapters.editor_note: Keep participial adjective use for later.

chapters.title: Canis currēns
chapters.story: A dog running through the gate follows a boy carrying a basket.
chapters.editor_note: The image needs clear simultaneous actions.

chapters.title: Recēnsiō X — Quid factum est?
chapters.story: A short account contrasts ongoing actions, completed passive events and persons acting.
chapters.editor_note: No new lexical or grammatical forms in the cumulative reading.

chapters.title: Līvia dīcit…
chapters.story: Līvia reports that a traveller is approaching the house.
chapters.editor_note: Keep tense of infinitive present; later readings can add perfect infinitives.

chapters.title: Nūntiō acceptō
chapters.story: After receiving news, the family begins a journey.
chapters.editor_note: One simple detached phrase, illustrated before/after.

chapters.title: Canis sequitur
chapters.story: The dog follows a friend who tries to speak to the family.
chapters.editor_note: Make deponent forms recognizable without teaching every principal part at once.

chapters.title: Recēnsiō XI — Iter nūntiī
chapters.story: A small original fable-like journey revisits participles, reports and deponents.
chapters.editor_note: Avoid unreviewed constructions; add a listening version only when verified.

chapters.title: Maior an minor?
chapters.story: The children compare two trees, two animals and two houses.
chapters.editor_note: Superlatives remain an optional explicitly marked later subtopic.

chapters.title: Manūs et portūs
chapters.story: People load boxes by hand at a harbour.
chapters.editor_note: Begin with two familiar cases, not an entire declension table.

chapters.title: Diēs et rēs
chapters.story: A problem at the harbour is resolved on a particular day.
chapters.editor_note: Reuse diēs and rēs before rarer fifth-declension vocabulary.

chapters.title: Recēnsiō XII — In portū
chapters.story: An original harbour story recycles comparisons, deponents and fourth/fifth declensions.
chapters.editor_note: Last full review before the bridge story.

chapters.title: Fābula prīma — Pōns ad librōs
chapters.story: An original fable about an animal, a friend and a helpful action opens a path to adapted classics.
chapters.grammar_focus: Affirmative purpose clause ut + present subjunctive
chapters.editor_note: First original bridge reading; no imported ancient text without source and licence checks.

maximum_new_lemmas_meaning: Upper bound 38 teaching chapters x 15; not the current planned lexical allocation or a verified introduced count
ledger_note: Historical seed audit for initial 50-chapter plan: title/grammar may differ from v2. Use 130-chapter manifest for active syllabus. All seeds require revalidation against authored Latin text.
